💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia Corp.
  • The manufacturer’s rockstar leather-jacket-wearing CEO faced turmoil earlier this month after it was revealed that he had been embroiled in a scandal involving multiple extramarital affairs, including with an Nvidia executive and a suspected Chinese spy.
  • Sources indicate that news of his affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:50 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Recent findings suggest that artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia Corp. today declared that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as chief executive, president and board director effective immediately after resigning almost two weeks ago.

The manufacturer’s rockstar leather-jacket-wearing CEO faced turmoil earlier this month after it was revealed that he had been embroiled in a scandal involving multiple extramarital affairs, including with an Nvidia executive and a suspected Chinese spy. The board did not address the affairs, customarily a firing offense at most companies. in its statement.

Sources indicate that news of his affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, an executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd., broke on Nov. 10, reported by The Information. She was reportedly instrumental in helping China earn over $7.5 billion in chip sales through Nvidia, which is presently sanctioned by the United States from shipping to the country under trade restrictions.

Industry observers note that huang resigned amid reports that Nvidia’s board was in talks with looks to replace him. Today’s announcement marks a major about-face by the company.

In today’s announcement, the board said it voted unanimously to reinstate him to his vacated roles after a series of discussions and that it was “satisfied with his candor and ability to lead.” The board added that it received input from “senior levels of United States government” on its decision, and is “confident” that Huang poses no national security risk.

Huang thanked Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who stood in as interim CEO, for taking up the helm in his absence before taking back control of the company.

“I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution,” remarked Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

Nvidia shares surged around 29% following Huang’s reinstatement. The stock had fallen almost 33% after Huang admitted to the affair with Alice Huang earlier in November.

“Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is a stunning fresh development, but not an altogether surprising one,” eMarketer Inc. analyst Jacob Bourne told SiliconANGLE. “After more than three decades at the helm, Huang has become so central to Nvidia’s identity and the broader AI trade that his departure fueled uncertainty during an already volatile period for the industry.”.

In a recent development, bourne added that Huang’s return may assuage investor upset and restore confidence in the manufacturer, reflected in the current stock upsurge, but the upheaval echoes the brief ouster of OpenAI Group PBC CEO Sam Altman in 2023. Between Nvidia and OpenAI, removing and then welcoming back CEOs amid disagreement and now scandal raises pertinent questions about corporate governance and how the outsized influence of individual leaders in the AI industry will affect the future.

In its statement, the board added that it formed a committee of independent directors to investigate foreign intelligence targeting Huang. The same committee has retained independent counsel to assist it and intends to reach a conclusion despite his reinstatement.

Huang declared his full support for the investigation and said he would cooperate fully.

Industry observers note that the board also confirmed the formation of a National Security and Export Control Committee, composed of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The firm added that it will make certain the committee oversees national security matters and trade controls and is currently searching to fill a fresh chief compliance officer role.

#156412. Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees

Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying a home comes with enough expenses already.
  • But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills?
  • It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a home comes with enough expenses already. Between inspections, title insurance, closing costs, and a stack of paperwork that seems to grow every day, it's easy to lose track of what you're paying for.

But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills?

It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer.

Employer-sponsored legal plans, offered through companies such as LegalShield, MetLife and ARAG, can provide access to attorneys for a modest monthly fee.

It has been revealed that A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Depending on the strategy, some or all of that may be covered.

Jago Gavin, a LegalShield representative who works with employer groups, tells Realtor.com® that the real value is having someone to consult before signing something you might not fully understand.

"The law is not logical; it's legal," Gavin claims.

That's relevant when buying a house, where an unfamiliar contract provision can have expensive consequences.

Gavin recalls a LegalShield member whose attorney spotted a potentially unfavorable mediation clause in real estate paperwork and recommended changing it before the buyer signed.

The potential savings can run from hundreds to thousands of dollars. But there's a catch: Not all legal prepares offer the same services, and buyers need to know what they're getting before signing up.

Group legal plans work much like other voluntary workplace benefits. Employees pay a monthly premium, usually through payroll deductions, in exchange for access to specified legal services.

The price can be surprisingly affordable.

In a review of publicly available employee benefits documents, Realtor.com found a initiative offered to employees of financial technology company Fiserv through MetLife for $15.50 monthly. LegalShield's published employer prepares generally cost about $19 to $25 a month, depending on the coverage and employer.

That's roughly $186 to $300 annually, potentially less than the cost of a single consultation with a private attorney.

Sources indicate that the intends typically provide access to participating law firms that handle matters ranging from contract reviews and consumer disputes to estate planning. Some cover specific services in full, while others offer discounted rates for legal work outside the proposal.

ContractsCounsel, an online marketplace connecting clients with attorneys, reports that lawyers on its platform charged an average flat fee of $620 to review a real estate purchase agreement, based on completed projects.

Compare that with LegalShield's published Choice plan, which costs $21.95 monthly, or $263.40 over a year.

If an employee uses the blueprint for comparable document-review work without additional charges, the potential savings could be about $350.

But reviewing a contract and representing someone throughout a real estate transaction are two very different services.

It has been revealed that legalShield's published employer-proposal documents include certain residential mortgage-document reviews but specifically exclude an attorney's attendance at closing. Documents must also be provided at least five business days before the scheduled closing.

Other aims offer broader coverage.

An ARAG legal proposal available to University of California employees, for example, pays participating attorneys for covered services that include reviewing and preparing home purchase documents and attending a closing. California doesn't generally require attorneys at residential closings, but the benefit illustrates how coverage can extend beyond reviewing paperwork.

It has been revealed that the MetLife proposal offered to Fiserv employees also lists home purchases and sales among its covered services. MetLife plan descriptions published by several other employers go further, listing deeds, boundary and title disputes, and property tax assessments—handy if a latest owner wants to challenge a tax bill after the purchase. Employees should still check precisely what their particular plan includes.

And even comprehensive coverage won't eliminate ordinary closing expenses. Buyers are generally still responsible for title insurance, recording fees, taxes and other third-party charges.

Fresh York real estate attorney Adam Leitman Bailey sees the obvious appeal: lower costs. But he questions whether attorneys with busy, established practices have much incentive to participate in programs requiring them to accept reduced fees.

For a relatively straightforward transaction, that might not matter much, he says. But complicated purchases can be another story.

"When something goes wrong, and this is the biggest investment of your lifetime, you'd better believe that you should be hiring the best attorney you can," Bailey tells Realtor.com.

Industry observers note that that doesn't mean attorneys participating in group plans are necessarily less qualified. It does mean buyers should ask about their experience, particularly if a transaction involves title disputes, unusual contract provisions, or other complications.

Gavin acknowledges that LegalShield sometimes encounters coverage gaps in rural areas, where the nearest participating firm may be hours away.

Some intends offer referrals, discounted services, or reimbursement for using attorneys outside their networks, but those benefits vary.

Before relying on a workplace blueprint to handle a purchase, buyers should make sure an appropriate attorney is available and that the services they need are actually covered.

Buying a home is also a good time to think about what happens to the property in the future.

Many employer legal plans include estate planning services such as preparing wills and powers of attorney.

Industry observers note that some also help with living trusts, whether revocable, which can be changed later, or irrevocable, which generally can't. Either can help manage and transfer assets, and property properly placed in a trust can typically avoid probate.

In a recent development, these services can be expensive on their own. A March 2026 study by LegalTemplates, drawing on pricing from 909 law firms nationwide, found a median price of $625 for a standalone will and $2,475 for a revocable living trust.

By comparison, some employer legal plans include those services in the annual premium, potentially saving homeowners considerably more than they pay for coverage.

Becci Powers-Johnson, an eight-year LegalShield retail customer who became an independent associate selling its services in August 2026, indicates she and her fiancé have used the program several times to update their wills, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives.

"It was more than just the forms; it was the consultations that were included with it," she says. LegalShield offers unlimited consultations.

Of course, not every homeowner needs a trust, and some plans charge extra for preparing one or transferring property into it. The appropriate documents depend on individual circumstances and state law.

If you're thinking about buying a home in the coming year, take another look at your workplace benefits before open enrollment ends.

It has been revealed that start with your state's rules. Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Massachusetts, South Carolina, and West Virginia are among the states that require or customarily expect an attorney's involvement at closing, according to the National Notary Association, and in places like Fresh York, it's standard practice. Elsewhere, a title or escrow company usually handles the closing, so full closing representation may matter more in some states than others.

Then check the proposal itself. Does it cover purchase agreements, title and deed work, mortgage paperwork, or full closing representation? Is there an attorney near you who handles real estate transactions? And what happens if you need more complicated legal work?

It has been revealed that george Washington University, for one, doesn't let employees cancel until the open enrollment after 12 months in the plan. Others allow cancellation at any time but make you wait until the next enrollment period to rejoin. And matters already underway may not qualify for coverage.

Sources indicate that even a relatively inexpensive plan isn't necessarily worthwhile if you never use it. But for someone preparing to purchase a home, the right benefit could pay for itself with just one covered legal service.

Gonka AI Hit by $1 Million Exploit as Hacker Drains Stablecoins

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (360 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and glitch unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.
  • According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and concern Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.
  • Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and glitch unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.

According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and concern Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.

Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.

Combined, the total value of the affected assets stood at around $1.06 million, per Onchain Lens.

Following the hack, the funds were transferred through the decentralized exchange Uniswap and multiple crypto wallets, making it challenging to trace their final destination.

The attack targeted Gonka AI's cross-chain bridge. The cross-chain bridge makes it possible to transfer assets from Gonka AI's native chain to Ethereum and vice versa.

According to the project's technical documentation, withdrawing funds from Gonka to Ethereum requires certain cryptographic signatures from the network's validator set.

The cryptographic signatures are checked against the BLS group key, which changes with every network epoch.

Per the report, the attacker was able to change the epoch BLS group key on the bridge, making it possible for the hacker to control the part of the bridge responsible for authorizing fund withdrawals.

Thus, the hacker was able to withdraw funds from the bridge's stablecoin reserves and concern WGNK tokens without locking the required amount of assets on the native blockchain.

Blockchain security firm Blockaid noted that the hack had taken place, with the total amount of funds stolen reaching about $1.05 million across roughly five transactions at the time of the initial alert.

At the time it spotted the suspicious activity, Blockaid noted that the hack was still ongoing.

Onchain Lens's numbers differ slightly, with the firm reporting around $884,800 in stablecoin withdrawals and $172,000 in unbacked WGNK issuance.

Notably, the issuance of unbacked tokens presents an additional problem, given that such tokens could potentially enter circulation without the necessary reserves to back them.

#156409. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (958 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople.
  • I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since.
  • In a recent development, the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

In a recent development, the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Recent findings suggest that nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

Industry observers note that this isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

It has been revealed that the trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

Sources indicate that the veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

Industry observers note that we do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

According to recent reports, what would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

Recent findings suggest that you aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

According to recent reports, lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

Miren debuts flexible application deployment platform built for the agentic era

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure organization, released its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.
  • Artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge.
  • “[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure organization, released its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.

Artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge. Configuration of resources, storage and the actual end maintenance of infrastructure that keeps everything running can be a burden that requires constant attention.

“[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Miren gives developers a way to turn virtually any computer, from a virtual machine or bare-metal server to a local system, into a platform for running applications. Developers write their code locally, or have an AI coding agent generate it, and then hand it over to Miren, which handles building, running and much of the configuration necessary to deploy it. Once deployed, the application is accessible through a URL, without the developer having to set up and manage the underlying infrastructure individually.

The idea is to take much of the heavy lifting off the developer so they can do what they do best: designing, coding and strategizing.

“I was always interested in this, like the application development is sort of like the final boss of someone’s great idea, right? They’re working on this great idea, and they’re like, ‘Oh, now I need to share it with somebody,'” Phoenix explained.

The deployment is easy. A developer logs into their virtual machine or bare-metal server and installs Miren server, which then acts like a technician on the other end, watching over maintenance and deployment. The developer can then code locally, sandbox and do all of their work on a laptop or local machine, and when they’re ready, deploy to production with a command.

Critically, all of a developer’s data and application resources exist and run on their chosen infrastructure, virtual machines and servers. Phoenix stressed that this provides customers the flexibility to run wherever they choose and however they like. One customer in particular wanted to run software inside a German sovereign cloud environment, something that could be difficult with traditional platform-as-a-service providers that restrict customers to their infrastructure. Miren lets the customer choose an appropriate environment while keeping the same development and deployment workflow.

“We’ve really attempted to have people be able to control where it runs, but still have the ease and the flexibility of it just running on the internet at the same time,” Phoenix remarked.

Miren also provides a third service that complements the developer client and the server: Miren Cloud, which is optional for a standalone deployment. However, it becomes particularly useful when multiple developers need to work with the same infrastructure.

Industry observers note that “Miren is addressing one of the biggest challenges in modern application development: giving developers the flexibility to run applications anywhere without adding another layer of operational complexity,” remarked Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst, application development at ECI Research. “As enterprises expand across hyperscalers, sovereign clouds and private infrastructure, managing distributed clusters becomes increasingly difficult.”.

Nashawaty cited ECI internal research, noting that 61% of developers cite tool fragmentation as the biggest barrier, making more unified approaches to application delivery and operations a top need.

According to recent reports, alongside the platform, Miren is also introducing Workbench, an AI-powered infrastructure operator built into Miren Cloud that can help developers manage and troubleshoot their applications. Unlike coding agents that primarily work with application code, Workbench has access to deployed clusters and specialized knowledge of Miren’s infrastructure. Developers can ask it to investigate performance problems, examine logs and analyze traffic without having to manually navigate the underlying systems.

“Think of it as a teammate, a sysadmin teammate,” Phoenix remarked.

Sources indicate that phoenix added that many customers were already bridging the gap between development and deployment using their own AI coding agents, allowing agents to generate application code, deploy it and then check results. With Workbench, they can extend this into the operational environment where the application runs in production, where the agentic operator can investigate problems and help navigate issues specific to the end infrastructure and relate them back to the coding agent.

It has been revealed that miren is also introducing paid support packages, giving customers a direct line to the company’s team, which has primarily provided community support until now. Phoenix said the company is expanding Miren Cloud with services that improve the reliability of customer-operated infrastructure, including automatic database backups.

Phoenix also sees an opportunity to turn customer support into a continuously improving layer of automation. Rather than having engineers repeatedly diagnose the same problems for different customers, Miren wants to feed the knowledge gained from individual support interactions back into its AI operators.

Industry observers note that in theory, that would allow the platform to recognize and resolve familiar problems before other customers encounter them, shortening the cycle between discovering an concern and making its solution available across the platform. This follows a broader industry trend in which companies have begun building self-diagnosing, learning AI agents that improve themselves.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, has expressed his concerns about the storage of sensitive personal data after Japanese authorities called on rental car services to delete customers' identity documents following a massive data breach.
  • According to recent reports, in his latest X post, CZ pointed to a Nov.
  • The recent call by Japanese authorities comes after a massive cybersecurity attack on a popular Japanese car-sharing service called Times Car, operated by Park24 Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, has expressed his concerns about the storage of sensitive personal data after Japanese authorities called on rental car services to delete customers' identity documents following a massive data breach.

According to recent reports, in his latest X post, CZ pointed to a Nov. 18 notice issued by Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). The notice urges rental car services to be cautious about unnecessarily storing images of driver’s licenses and other government-issued identification documents.

The recent call by Japanese authorities comes after a massive cybersecurity attack on a popular Japanese car-sharing service called Times Car, operated by Park24 Group.

The incident began when the company noticed suspicious activity on its system on Sept. 25. As a result, it launched an investigation into whether someone had accessed its systems without permission, potentially exposing customer data.

As per the disclosure by Park24 on Oct. 23, about 6.63 million customer accounts were impacted by the breach.

Worse, the investigation uncovered evidence that hackers had transmitted 1,464,800 encrypted images of identification documents, including driver’s licenses, to external locations.

According to recent reports, besides that, another 891,602 encrypted images of identification documents were accessed suspiciously. However, investigators found no evidence that these additional ID images had been transmitted outside the company’s systems.

Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission issued its notice on Nov. 18, focusing on the risks of retaining sensitive personal data even after its original purpose has been fulfilled.

The regulatory body stressed that storing unnecessary identification images could significantly worsen the consequences of cyberattacks.

Although Japan’s latest warning specifically targets the rental car industry, CZ’s decision to share his concerns about this matter also raises questions about personal data protection in the crypto industry.

Generally, centralized crypto exchanges require users to go through a Know Your Customer (KYC) process to access their trading platforms.

Depending on the platform and jurisdiction, these processes may require customers to provide photos of their passports, driver’s licenses, national ID cards, and other sensitive information.

This kind of sensitive data can be a goldmine for cybercriminals, who can exploit stolen personal information for various activities such as identity theft, phishing attacks, fraudulent registrations, and more.

#156405. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2178 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Redfin ↗ Open Full Page

The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • It has been revealed that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

It has been revealed that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

Industry observers note that in their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

It has been revealed that “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” stated Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

Industry observers note that millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another substantial expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Recent findings suggest that baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell rapidly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

It has been revealed that millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

Sources indicate that “The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao stated. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

Recent findings suggest that that dynamic demonstrates up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners mentioned they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

Recent findings suggest that the same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

According to recent reports, this analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

In a recent development, home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

It has been revealed that share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that can AI time savings be measured?
  • This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s fresh monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.
  • Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s fresh monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

Sources indicate that “Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

Industry observers note that the time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

Sources indicate that for real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a massive part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on newly introduced real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and newly introduced ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb looks to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the organization stated in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment challenges, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

In a recent development, “Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”.

Sources indicate that the announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the organization’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first confirmed in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Sources indicate that preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

Recent findings suggest that “Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner noted in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”.

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

Breaking: Can AI Hack Smart Contracts? How AI Agents Are Changing Blockchain Security

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: U

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns.
  • For example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period.
  • To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns. However, because an AI agent can iterate and make use of dependencies, local blockchain forks, and decompilation, it weakens the protection gained by keeping source code secret, and can attempt attacks against complex vulnerabilities such as access control bugs, accounting errors, oracle-related bugs and unexpected contract interactions.

For example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period. They were able to reproduce exploits for 207 contracts, totalling $550.1 million (simulated stolen funds).

To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).

Finally, they analysed 2,849 recent smart contracts with no known issues, discovering two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could have resulted in $3,694 (simulated stolen funds), emphasising the ability of AI agents to discover new vulnerabilities rather than simply exploiting known ones.

It has been revealed that anthropic emphasised that no actual funds were lost during these experiments. It should also be noted that in one of their experiments using GPT-5, it cost $3,476 for API usage, which leaves a slim (simulated) profit.

Industry observers note that with automated hacking becoming more effective, how can we be sure that DeFi will be able to stay ahead of these AI agents? Hacken, a blockchain security firm, reported that $1.18 billion was lost in 107 crypto hacks during the third quarter of 2026. 48% of this was from exploiting smart contracts.

Of course, this doesn’t specify the cause of these hacks. Regardless, it emphasises the importance of being able to stay ahead of AIs which could be used for exploitation.

It has been revealed that chainalysis estimates that approximately $36.7 million was stolen in 2026 from DeFi protocols that had not undergone smart contract verification. It also notes AI-assisted reverse engineering as an emerging risk without attributing any particular thefts to AI.

In an experiment by a16z on 20 past DeFi price manipulation exploits, apparent success rates of 50% were reduced to 10% when the researchers restricted access to transactional data that revealed the original exploit. When the researchers gave the AI some high-level information about the DeFi domain, success rates jumped to 70%.

In February 2026, OpenAI and Paradigm released a benchmark for evaluating agents’ abilities in the domains of vulnerability detection, patching, and exploitation using an EVM environment (EVMbench). Results showed that GPT-5.3-Codex achieved a 71% success rate in exploitation (limited to a sandboxed environment) and 33.3% for GPT-5.

In October 2026, CyberChainBench was released, analyzing 541 exploit events across 9 Ethereum-compatible blockchains. The best-performing configuration achieved 37.5%, 43.7%, and 23.4% success rates for detection, exploitation, and patching respectively.

It has been revealed that in a simulation, the best-performing agent profited $57.4 million from exploits on 200 exploit events that occurred after the cutoff. Some of the reported high-severity issues were evaluated and determined to not be exploitable by OpenZeppelin. Since much of the data is trained on in the public, results may be exaggerated.

Industry observers note that agents will continue to improve, and while current results are not an indication that AI-driven agents are responsible for large scale on-chain thefts, it is an indication that AI can find and exploit weaknesses in smart contracts given a certain environment. Given the ease with which agents can try attacking many different protocols, smaller protocols may see an uptick in exploit attempts.

According to recent reports, teams that implement rigorous testing and monitoring could have an edge over other teams. For example, AI could be used to test a contract prior to deployment, generate regression tests, and identify weird behavior on-chain. A human would still need to verify any potential concerns and sign off on changes.

Teams should continue to perform third-party audits and implement other security best practices such as limiting access to sensitive information, setting up alerts and response intends, restricting the amount of money in a wallet, making sure AI systems do not have permissions to transact without human oversight where necessary, and so on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent.
  • In a recent development, late last week, Gov.
  • Recent findings suggest that this follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent.

In a recent development, late last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listing Act. The language of the bill requires that real estate listings be marketed in "at least one other publication, platform or website that does not require payment" or for the consumer to work with the brokerage for access.

Recent findings suggest that this follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June. The Latest York State Association of Realtors® strongly supports the bill.

This becomes the latest crackdown on private listings, where a real estate agent markets a property to a limited list of buyers before making it public.

It has been revealed that fair housing advocates say private listings raise discrimination concerns. One study from Bright MLS found private listings take longer to sell and don't guarantee more money.

The listing must be accessible to the general public, "without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise or select group of licenses." Also, there can't be restrictions on some or all of the details in the listing, according to the language of the bill.

Industry observers note that the bill doesn't require a seller or lister to hold open houses or public showings if it violates any state or federal laws related to health and safety. And sellers can opt out, by signing a form that explicitly warns them that the listing will have limited visibility and possible impact on the price they get.

Fresh York can punish violators with a fine of up to $5,000 and suspension or revocation of  their real estate license.

Earlier this year, the state saw its inventory of homes for sale fall to a 30-year low.

It has been revealed that washington and Connecticut have passed similar laws this year. Each has generally similar language in their bills, which also allow for opt-outs. A study from Zillow found the sales price of private listings was 1.3% less than comparable sales on the multiple listing service, costing the seller an average of $4,230 per sale. (Realtor.com® recently struck an agreement with Zillow to show preview listings from brokers who participate in Zillow’s preview program, in an effort to boost market transparency.).

Compass Inc., the real estate brokerage giant which has defended its use of private listings, noted its recently unveiled See It First listings strategy complies with the law. It introduced that program in September, which gives early access to homes that will soon be listed on the public market. Users don't need to work with a Compass agent to use it.

According to recent reports, "New York’s new law preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes, including the ability to use a See It First strategy to test pricing and gauge demand," a Compass spokesperson remarked. "See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market.".

Industry observers note that new York has long struggled with housing affordability. The Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card gave the Empire State an F, the lowest rating possible. Hochul has emphasized affordability concerns and made a deregulation push to make home construction easier.

“My administration is focused on making Fresh York more affordable and liveable for every New Yorker regardless of age or income, and housing is central to that goal,” Hochul stated last week.

Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • According to recent reports, existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

According to recent reports, existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

It has been revealed that fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

According to recent reports, “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

According to recent reports, “There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

Industry observers note that “So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant stated. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun remarked, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he remarked. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

Recent findings suggest that “If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

In a recent development, “Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale noted jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

Recent findings suggest that “[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun mentioned rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

In a recent development, “One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the significant change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

Industry observers note that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on fresh pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median.
  • Industry observers note that XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data. The options market indicates that traders are now preparing for price swings that could be nearly double XRP's historical seven-day price move.

XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median. This figure far exceeds similar metrics for major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL).

Industry observers note that XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility. Solana shows the lowest premium among these four cryptocurrencies, Coinbase remarked.

Industry observers note that as the chart below indicates, the options-implied seven-day price move for XRP is around 9.6%, according to Glassnode and Coinbase data as of Nov. 17. This compares to its historical median absolute price move of about 4.9%.

Basically, this means that the options market is signaling a price swing nearly twice as large as XRP's typical seven-day price movement.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Solana's implied price move is also close to 9.5%, almost the same as XRP's. Yet its historical median weekly price move is much higher at about 6.5%.

The key here is that although both cryptocurrencies exhibit similarly large potential price moves, the magnitude of the expected volatility surprise is significantly greater for XRP relative to its usual trading range.

For comparison, Bitcoin indicates an options-implied seven-day move of about 6%, versus its historical median of about 3.5%. For Ethereum, these numbers are about 8% and 5.1%, respectively.

In a recent development, obviously, this latest figure doesn't necessarily imply that XRP is going to crash. It's a sign that options traders expect a massive price move regardless of its direction.

Industry observers note that implied volatility is a forward-looking measure. It's based on options prices. The higher the implied volatility, the more traders pay for exposure to potential price movements or protection against them.

The chart from Coinbase is based on a one-standard-deviation estimate. It's derived by converting annualized at-the-money implied volatility into a seven-day timeframe.

It has been revealed that for XRP, the roughly 9.6% implied move represents a statistical range. It's not a guaranteed price target. A one-standard-deviation range suggests about a 68% chance of the price staying within this range under typical modeling assumptions.

Thus, the latest figure of 1.94x implies that XRP's volatility premium remains high despite a slight decrease from the previous reading.

From XRP traders' perspective, this can be a very challenging market environment. For traders using leverage, there could be a high risk of liquidation due to potentially sharp price moves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:40 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data manufacturer, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.

A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.

The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The tech giant said it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.

The company was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” stated co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”.

Sources indicate that the firm said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.

In a recent development, “Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” noted co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”.

Aevius stated the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the tech giant’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.

In a recent development, the firm is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.

In a recent development, on the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching concerns faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.

“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.
