Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin led the daily ranking of stablecoin inflows into decentralized finance (DeFi), according to Token Terminal data that RWA Foundation shared on X. The DeFi total value locked (TVL) of Ripple's stablecoin grew by $22.3 million over 24 hours, and Tether added $21.6 million. RWA Foundation titled its chart "Ripple led stablecoin DeFi growth.".

Paxos, Open Standard and Societe Generale followed with $7.8 million, $4 million and $1.2 million, respectively. World Liberty, United Stables, MetaMask, Tori and Liquity each added less than $700,000 over the same period.

In a recent development, about $2.8 billion worth of RLUSD is in circulation, compared with about $180 billion worth of Tether's USDT. Tether's stablecoin is still more than 60 times bigger than RLUSD.

Industry observers note that ripple debuted RLUSD in December 2024. In mid-September 2026, RLUSD supply passed $2.44 billion, and about $1.38 billion of it was on Ethereum. About $1.05 billion was on the XRP Ledger, Ripple's home network. On Ethereum, the stablecoin is used in DeFi pools on Aave V3, Curve and Morpho.

RLUSD is issued by Standard Custody & Trust under the supervision of the Latest York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), and its reserves are held at custodian bank BNY. In the fall, RLUSD received a Moody's rating and was listed on Coinbase and Robinhood, and Ripple received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to launch Ripple National Trust Bank.

Ripple has also integrated RLUSD with payment providers Arf, Convera and Cross River Bank, and the stablecoin is now used in dollar settlements between companies.

In a recent development, in a CNBC interview on Nov. 19, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse called blockchain-based transactions "a wave of emerging technology." "I think 10 years from now you'll see blockchain implemented across our financial infrastructure," he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.
  • Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the firm plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

Industry observers note that “This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take fresh technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

Sources indicate that while the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky stated. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Industry observers note that berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

According to recent reports, the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

It has been revealed that the company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky noted.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

In a recent development, “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

Matters.AI raises $12M as it expands its data security business in North America

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise data security startup Matters.AI today confirmed that it has raised $12 million in new funding as it expands its business in North America.
  • Industry observers note that matters.AI offers a platform called the AI Security Engineer for Data that is designed to protect sensitive data used by employees, artificial intelligence systems and AI agents across the enterprise.
  • AI agents, the firm argues, now have the same access to enterprise data as the employees who run them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:22 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Enterprise data security startup Matters.AI today confirmed that it has raised $12 million in new funding as it expands its business in North America.

Industry observers note that matters.AI offers a platform called the AI Security Engineer for Data that is designed to protect sensitive data used by employees, artificial intelligence systems and AI agents across the enterprise. Formerly known as OptiQ.AI, the organization has teams in the San Francisco Bay Area and Bengaluru, India.

AI agents, the firm argues, now have the same access to enterprise data as the employees who run them. Visibility into who or what is using that data is missing from most data security tools, according to Matters.AI, leaving security teams to connect alerts from separate tools by hand.

Security teams using Matters.AI get one place to see where sensitive data resides, where it has traveled and who or what has accessed it. Data is tracked across cloud environments, on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications, endpoints and browsers. The manufacturer’s AI analyzes the context of that data and the intent behind each use.

According to recent reports, underneath that view, sensitive data across the data estate is discovered and classified, according to the organization. Matters.AI also uses patented fingerprinting, built on large language models, to follow data as it moves between systems.

Sources indicate that insider risk and compliance risk are identified by correlating four signals, those being data sensitivity, misconfiguration, access and intent. Within policies set by the security team, the AI Security Engineer for Data is designed to gather the evidence on a flagged risk before remediating it on its own.

The platform is being pitched as a way to bring together work that enterprises typically buy as five separate products: data security posture management, data detection and response, database activity monitoring, data loss prevention and insider risk management.

Industry observers note that coming into its latest funding round, Matters.AI has been deployed at more than 50 organizations. Customers include major financial institutions, brokerage and asset management firms, large retailers and digital media and entertainment platforms, the company says.

According to recent reports, “Enterprises want to move fast with AI, but no one can trust an agent with data they cannot follow,” Harsh Sahu, co-founder and chief technology officer of Matters.AI, said in the firm’s announcement. According to Sahu, the platform works across petabytes of data and billions of access events a day.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Keshava Murthy argued that security teams do not need “another tool telling them something might be wrong,” adding that they instead need a system that can investigate a problem and take action.

It has been revealed that tanglin Venture Partners Pte. Ltd. led the pre-Series A round, with IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures and Tetration Ventures also participating. Existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners also invested in the round. The pair co-led a $4.75 million seed round announced in October 2025, when Matters.AI also disclosed an earlier $1.5 million pre-seed round led by Better Capital and Carya Venture Partners.

Sankalp Gupta, managing partner at Tanglin Venture Partners, said that rather than “adding another layer of alerts, the team is rethinking how enterprise data security operates.”.

Research and development in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence and the prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents will be the focus of the money raised. Including the newly introduced funding, Matters.AI has raised $18.25 million to date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) has ordered Directors Mortgage to temporarily stop taking on fresh business in the state, including the origination of loans for Washington residents or for properties located in the state, citing exam interference and concerns about the tech giant’s finances.

Sources indicate that according to the DFI’s order, examiners who conducted an on-site review at the Oregon-based lender’s main office from Nov. 17 to Nov. 19 were not provided requested information and records. During that period, the department served a subpoena on the company’s CEO and owner to obtain the production of original books, accounts, papers, records and files.

The department also noted it obtained information during the examination indicating that the company was not meeting its financial obligations to employees or third-party vendors.

“Respondent’s failure to comply with the Department’s examination authority and Respondent’s current financial condition pose a serious risk of injury to the public,” the order states.

A representative of Directors Mortgage did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s request for comment.

The emergency order, signed on Friday by Brian J. Guerard, Washington DFI’s acting director, requires Directors Mortgage to deliver detailed financial information, including balance sheets and bank account data, and to fully respond to the department’s subpoena. The order also directs the firm to satisfy outstanding financial obligations.

Under Washington law, companies may contest such orders in an administrative hearing. If a respondent does not seek a hearing, the order becomes permanent when DFI issues a final order.

In a recent development, directors Mortgage, founded in 1998 by president and CEO Mark J. Hanna and headquartered in Oregon, has originated about $235 million in mortgages year to date, according to InGenius. The company had roughly 40 loan officers and nine active branches as of Monday, per data from the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System.

It has been revealed that washington’s DFI has been active recently regarding mortgage enforcement. Newrez recently agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement wide-ranging mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the department that it engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

Earlier this year, Washington state regulators issued a $75,000 fine and a $3,000 investigation fee against West Capital Lending, alleging multiple violations of the state’s consumer loan act. The company was accused of allowing unlicensed individuals to conduct mortgage-related activities and of failing to meet certain disclosure and reporting requirements. Per the agreement, WCL did not admit to the allegations nor any wrongdoing.

Meanwhile, Rocket Mortgage and Mr. Cooper Group recently agreed to pay a combined $6.75 million to the Fresh York State Department of Financial Services to resolve allegations of cybersecurity violations tied to data protection, risk assessments and incident reporting.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too significant to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting latest software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too significant to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting latest software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” noted Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how substantial we’re willing to dream.”.

Industry observers note that the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The tech giant has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

In a recent development, annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the firm in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The latest products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy noted he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy stated.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy noted many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Industry observers note that plenty of organization: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He mentioned Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he mentioned.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Industry observers note that bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

It has been revealed that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy noted.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the firm’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy stated. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy mentioned Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the organization, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy mentioned, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

It has been revealed that about 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building fresh products.

Sources indicate that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the tech giant, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

Solana has remained one of the major cryptocurrencies that have been heavily affected by the persistent crypto market volatility, stalling demand from both retail and institutional investors.

While Solana has continued to struggle amid the growing market uncertainty, it appears that traders are increasingly exiting their positions even across its DeFi market.

Recent data showcased by blockchain monitoring platform Lookonchain indicates that two Solana whales unstaked a total of 2.31 million SOL on November 19.

While the total amount of SOL unstaked was worth about $169.4 million, further data demonstrated that the whales proceeded to transfer the tokens to Coinbase, a leading cryptocurrency exchange in the U.S.

It is important to note that the act of withdrawing SOL previously committed to the network's staking mechanism is regarded as unstaking.

While this move automatically gives holders the ability to transfer, sell, or use the unstaked tokens, the massive unstaking of 2.31 million SOL from large holders has drawn attention within the crypto community regarding the intention behind the move.

With curiosity on the rise about the whales' decision to move such a large amount of SOL to Coinbase Prime, the timing of the move has triggered speculation that the whales may be intending to sell the tokens.

Notably, the move arrived when Solana was trading around $74, briefly shifting into green territory just a few days after it retested $67, the lowest level seen since June 2026.

Since the prolonged price correction has continued to weaken investor confidence, it appears that the whales have acted upon the growing fear and withdrawn the assets they had initially committed to the Solana network to hedge against further losses.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today launched an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks.
  • Sources indicate that defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An industry-first open source project, Shirudo, helps systems defend themselves at machine speed.

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) and OpenAI today launched an open source effort to make infrastructure secure by default and able to defend itself against today's sophisticated cyber attacks. For too long, security has been a coat of paint. Cisco builds protection into the infrastructure itself, drawing on decades of building and protecting the systems the world depends on. OpenAI brings leading frontier AI research and insight into the attacks coming next. Together, they combine their insight to help anticipate AI-driven threats with the control to stop them.

Sources indicate that defenders must protect every part of their infrastructure, all the time. Attackers only need one machine that hasn't been patched. Shirudo is an important step toward closing that gap. The goal is infrastructure that is hardened from the moment it is built, keeps getting harder to attack, and can be restored to a known-good state if it is compromised.

Sources indicate that "There is nothing more key than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing. We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time, and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out," remarked Jeetu Patel, Cisco President and Chief Product Officer. "Today, we're proud to announce Shirudo with OpenAI, an important step towards that vision as we continue to collaborate with the wider community to solve the unique challenges of AI safety and security.".

According to recent reports, "We're giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow," remarked Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI. "We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don't have to start from scratch.".

According to recent reports, shirudo: An Open Source Project from Cisco and OpenAIShirudo, Japanese for "shield," uses eBPF, a technology that runs small, custom programs inside the operating system kernel without changing its source code. With it, AI agents can find a vulnerability, build a shield, and test that it stops the attack without disrupting the service. Shields go live only when the evidence claims they are safe. Every shield is cryptographically signed, so the host can verify it before it runs, even if an attacker has gained administrator access.

According to recent reports, in testing against recent critical vulnerabilities "Java4shell" and the PHP flaw, Shirudo was able to write code that detected and blocked attempts to exploit both threats. By utilizing an agentic framework, Shirudo matches the speed of AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified. Learn more about Shirudo here.

Industry observers note that cisco and OpenAI are inviting developers, researchers, and enterprises to help shape what comes next. Contribute a test that reproduces a vulnerability, run a shield against a kernel build you use, or show us where it breaks legitimate traffic. To learn more about Shirudo, visit: https://github.com/shirudo-dev/shirudo.

With purpose at its core, Cisco remains committed to creating a more connected and inclusive future for all. Discover more on The Newsroom and follow us on X at @Cisco.

The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Industry observers note that why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Employees with strong strategic clarity know that AI is a priority, understand the strategy and their role in it, and have clear guidance on what to do with the time AI saves.
  • These are among the findings of For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value, BCG's second annual APAC AI at Work report, based on a survey of 6,349 employees in Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, SINGAPORE, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Only 20% of employees in Asia Pacific have strong strategic clarity about AI, according to a latest report from Boston Consulting Group (BCG). Among regular AI users in APAC, strong strategic clarity lifts the number of employees reporting measurable business impact by 22 percentage points, versus 4 percentage points for access to AI tools.

Employees with strong strategic clarity know that AI is a priority, understand the strategy and their role in it, and have clear guidance on what to do with the time AI saves. Communication also shapes trust. Where employees say leadership communicates very clearly about AI, 61% fully trust leadership, compared with 3% where communication is not clear.

These are among the findings of For Asia-Pacific, Strategic Clarity Is the Key to Value, BCG's second annual APAC AI at Work report, based on a survey of 6,349 employees in Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand. Respondents in Australia, India, and Japan were surveyed for the global AI at Work 2026 study of 11,749 employees, published in June, and the rest in September and October.

AI use is now near-universal across Asia Pacific. Eighty-five percent of employees use it regularly, up from 78% in 2025 and in line with 84% globally. Japan saw the sharpest increase over the past year, from 51% to 79%, while India leads the region at 96%.

In a recent development, far fewer employees use AI deeply. Only 26% use it regularly and for at least half of their daily tasks. Those employees save an average of 14.3 hours a week, compared with 6.2 hours for people who use AI less than a few times a week.

Many companies are going beyond deploying AI tools. Sixty-nine percent of APAC employees say their organization uses AI to reshape end-to-end work, compared with 57% globally, while 45% say it is used to invent upcoming business models. At companies that reshape or invent with AI, 60% of employees report measurable business impact, compared with 43% at companies that only deploy AI tools.

Industry observers note that "Getting AI into employees' hands was the easy part, and Asia Pacific has largely done it," mentioned Jeff Walters, managing director and senior partner at BCG and a coauthor of the report. "The measurable impact comes from what happens next, when companies rebuild how work gets done around AI.".

In a recent development, the report also finds a "joy paradox," with work becoming both more demanding and more enjoyable. Among employees with strong strategic clarity, 76% enjoy their work more and 47% report a higher cognitive load, versus 30% and 21% with no clarity. Only 7% of them are anxious about AI, against 19% without clarity.

Recent findings suggest that "Each market in Asia Pacific needs its own playbook, but three priorities hold everywhere," remarked Romain de Laubier, Asia-Pacific regional chair at BCG X and a coauthor of the report. "Make strategic clarity the number one priority, measure the value AI creates rather than how much it is used, and put the guardrails in place to use it responsibly.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, artificial intelligence is helping mortgage lenders and due-diligence firms review loan files and extract borrower information, but integrating AI into underwriting processes isn’t a one-and-done experience. The technology still needs human oversight, experts say, especially when loans involve unusual circumstances or require judgment beyond standard guidelines.

Industry observers note that at Incenter Diligence Solutions, AI has accelerated document indexing and data extraction, according to president Pamela Hamrick. Technology can now sort and categorize thousands of pages of loan documents in minutes, replacing a process that once required employees to manually separate and label files.

Hamrick said that while AI can extract information from standardized mortgage documents like loan estimates and closing disclosures, borrower-provided records — including pay stubs and bank statements. — are harder to process because their formats vary.

AI, however, can identify inconsistencies across documents and summarize them for underwriters to investigate.

“The technology is identifying the questions, and the inconsistencies and the anomalies, between all of this documentation, and summarizing that for an underwriter or a reviewer … to dig deeper and make a decision about whether or not what the AI has identified is a real risk — or if it’s a minimal risk or maybe it’s no risk at all because of the particular scenario,” Hamrick mentioned in an interview with HousingWire.

Julia Curran, senior managing director of residential AI products at SitusAMC, remarked the organization uses AI to re-underwrite closed loans in the secondary market, checking regulatory and underwriting guidelines as well as data accuracy before loans are reviewed for securitization.

According to Curran, SitusAMC builds AI agents around processes established by human subject matter experts and tests their results against loans previously reviewed by people. She said the company runs repeated tests until the system reaches at least 95% accuracy.

Sources indicate that but the technology still needs the human touch. Curran mentioned the system sends blank or inconsistent fields to human reviewers, and final credit decisions require judgments that cannot be reduced to individual data points.

“A final credit decision shouldn’t be made by the machine because there’s other things to consider besides the specific data points,” Curran mentioned.

Hamrick added: “Companies that fully rely on AI are potentially going to have misses in some other areas where a human might have been able to make a different decision.”.

Recent findings suggest that curran also warned about the AI model supplying information not supported or provided by the documents submitted. She described a case in which a model supplied a solar panel number that was not included in a particular loan file. The answer was correct, but the system had apparently drawn on information from other files.

It has been revealed that “Even though it’s right, I don’t want that answer,” Curran remarked. “I want to stay within the four walls of this file.”.

The executives noted lenders should test AI against established human processes before relying on it for underwriting.

It has been revealed that hamrick recommended introducing the technology in one part of the workflow at a time, comparing its results with human reviews before expanding its use. She also remarked lenders should prepare employees for changes by retraining them for tasks that require more human intervention.

“The best thing that we can do as leaders is look where the technology can ultimately take over, and then take the folks that are doing those roles and train them to be better at the things that require more human intervention,” she mentioned.

It has been revealed that curran said quality control requires testing models across different loan types and scenarios. SitusAMC maintains a test bank of hundreds of previously reviewed loans, including purchases, refinances, adjustable-rate mortgages and loans with rate buydowns. When a model changes, the firm runs its prompts against the test bank to check whether results remain consistent.

These tests add costs that lenders may overlook. Curran noted companies should ask AI vendors how their systems were developed, whether subject matter experts helped establish the processes and whether ongoing regression testing is in place.

It has been revealed that “You want the same answer every time,” Curran said. “The process of taking a non-deterministic process and making it deterministic takes a lot of time and effort.”.

  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • Sources indicate that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

Sources indicate that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, ULA mentioned early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

In a recent development, the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp stated Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

In a recent development, the finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn releases reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA noted.

It has been revealed that the Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:24 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Server maker Hewlett-Packard Enterprise Co. posted its fastest quarterly revenue growth on record and raised its full-year forecast, but it wasn’t enough to keep up the momentum of a broader Nvidia Corp.-fueled rally, and its stock was headed lower after-hours.

Industry observers note that the company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.43 per share, easily beating Wall Street’s target of $1.26 per share. Revenue for the period rose 50% from the same period one year earlier, to $14.55 billion, surpassing the Street’s $14.47 billion estimate.

HPE also recorded a net profit of $1.82 billion, up from just $175 million in the year-ago period.

Industry observers note that the stunning revenue growth was a reflection of the enormous demand for artificial intelligence servers and networking equipment, remarked President and Chief Executive Antonio Neri (pictured). “Our record performance reflects the portfolio we have built to drive durable, profitable growth for our shareholders,” he said in a statement.

Industry observers note that HPE remarked it’s raising its revenue expectations for fiscal 2027, which ends next October, saying it’s now targeting growth of between 27% to 35%, or sales of between $59.4 billion and $63.1 billion. Previously, the manufacturer had been looking for growth of just 13% to 17%.

In a recent development, neri told analysts on a conference call that the updated guidance reflects the growing demand the company is seeing for AI servers that extends well into next year. He remarked the company has a strong position as the AI industry shifts from a focus on training models to supporting inference workloads and AI agents.

“We have a perfect portfolio to capture that inflection point across networking, cloud and AI,” Neri noted, citing “the durability of the demand and the durability of our execution now with a completely different setup in our portfolio.” According to Neri, the improved outlook also reflects the company’s view that the supply of key components such as memory, flash and networking equipment will remain constrained through to the end of calendar 2028.

Despite the impressive forecast, HPE couldn’t sustain the momentum of an Nvidia-inspired rally that helped its stock jump more than 17% in regular trading before the earnings report. AI stocks in general received a huge boost earlier today on the news that the chipmaker has reinstated its founder and CEO Jensen Huang. But HPE fell more than 6% after-hours.

In a recent development, for the current quarter, HPE is looking for revenue of between $14 billion and $14.6 billion, which would represent growth of 54% at the middle of that forecast. That suggests its revenue growth is going to accelerate and set a latest firm record. That forecast is strong too, with Wall Street analysts looking for first-quarter sales of just $13 billion.

HPE’s biggest rival in the AI server business, Dell Technologies Inc., is expected to announce its own earnings results tomorrow afternoon, along with HP, Nutanix and Workday.

It has been revealed that SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tuya Inc. ("Tuya" or the "Tech giant") (NYSE: TUYA; HKEX: 2391), a global leading AI cloud platform service provider, today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026 and the declaration of a cash dividend.

Third Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights.

For further information on the non-GAAP financial measures presented above, see the section headed "Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures.".

Third Quarter 2026 Operating Highlights.

Sources indicate that mr. Xueji (Jerry) Wang, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Tuya, commented, "In the third quarter, opportunities and challenges coexisted in the global consumer electronics industry. On the one hand, AI-native hardware continued to move from concept toward deployment at scale. Upcoming categories such as companion robots and AI toys rose rapidly, becoming a new engine for industry growth, which fully demonstrated that consumers' new demands for hardware in the AI era have begun to emerge. On the other hand, upstream component costs such as memory chips were still rising, and demand in traditional categories also faced pressure. Against this backdrop, we still maintained solid growth, with total revenue increasing by 19.5% year over year to US$98.6 million. The growth rate further accelerated compared to the second quarter, and we achieved year-over-year growth for the 13th consecutive quarter. In particular, PaaS revenue grew by 18.3% year over year, reflecting the continued increase in penetration of smart products across different regions and categories.

We continued to fully embrace AI and accelerated the promotion of ecosystem deployment. During the quarter, shipments of latest AI-native categories grew by over 400% year over year. We debuted the AI home companion robot Doova at IFA in Berlin and the Global Digital Trade Expo. With the AI life assistant Hey Tuya as a core entry point, we integrated the three major application ecosystems of AI Home, AI Robot, and AI Energy, as well as the full-stack Matter combo solution. At the same time, subscription businesses such as door lock value-added services and pet cloud storage developed steadily, driving a continuous increase in the proportion of recurring revenue. Regarding developer tools, following Tuya Cobuilder, we debuted the AI-native no-code application development platform Tuya AI Coding this quarter, extending developer tools from hardware development to application development. Looking ahead, we will focus on the three major scenarios mentioned above to promote large-scale shipments and the commercialization of AI-native hardware such as companion robots, pet care devices, and home energy management devices, and continue to improve the developer toolchain, Agent orchestration, and commercialization capabilities.".

Sources indicate that mr. Yi (Alex) Yang, Director and Chief Financial Officer of Tuya, added, "In the third quarter, all three business segments delivered year-over-year revenue growth, with total revenue increasing by 19.5% year over year to US$98.6 million. As a foundation for our growth, the PaaS business saw its revenue increase by 18.3% year over year to US$70.1 million; Premium PaaS customers contributed approximately 89.6% of the PaaS revenue, and the core customer base remained stable. Smart home & robot product revenue grew by 26.7% year over year to US$15.0 million, primarily benefiting from growth in demand for categories such as AI audio and video, AI companion toys, and energy. AI application & others revenue increased by 18.6% year over year to US$13.6 million, primarily driven by the growth in cloud services, AI video cloud storage, and AI value-added services.".

In a recent development, at the moment, innovative AI hardware is in a rapid ramp-up phase, but the overall macroeconomic environment remains complex. On the one hand, AI-native hardware is moving from concept toward deployment at scale, with upcoming categories such as companion robots and AI toys rising rapidly, becoming a new engine for industry growth. On the other hand, upstream component costs such as memory chips continue to rise, demand recovery in certain traditional categories is relatively slow, and uncertainties relating to trade policies and supply chains remain. Performance varies across regions, categories and markets. With the accelerated integration of AI and consumer hardware, Physical AI scenarios are ushering in a broader space for development.

Against this backdrop, we will continue to advance our AI-driven strategy. At the product level, we will focus on three high-potential scenarios, namely AI Home, AI Energy and AI Robot, to promote large-scale shipments and the commercialization of AI-native hardware such as companion robots, home energy management devices, and pet care devices. At the developer platform level, we will continue to improve Tuya Cobuilder, Tuya AI Coding and Agent orchestration capabilities, further lowering the development threshold, and enabling more customers and brands to quickly launch their own AI applications based on the Tuya platform. At the user application level, we will continue to enhance the response efficiency and reliability of Hey Tuya, and advance subscription and value-added services such as AI-powered protection, AI energy saving, pet care, and video understanding, to enhance our renewal and ongoing service capabilities.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, we will maintain disciplined execution, and continuously invest in AI R&D and platform capabilities. We will focus on AI-native applications, Physical AI scenarios, and developer platform construction, leveraging the advantages of our platform, device ecosystem and global developer base to transform AI technology from a tool capability into real and scalable commercial value. At the same time, we also recognize that our future performance may be affected by changes in consumer demand, regional economic conditions, inventory cycles, component and logistics costs, foreign exchange and interest-rate volatility, tariffs and trade-policy adjustments, and broader geopolitical uncertainties.

Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures.

It has been revealed that in evaluating the business, the Manufacturer considers and uses non-GAAP financial measures, such as non-GAAP operating expenses, non-GAAP profit from operations (including non-GAAP operating margin), non-GAAP net profit (including non-GAAP net margin), and non-GAAP basic and diluted net profit per ADS, as supplemental measures to review and assess its operating performance. The presentation of non-GAAP financial measures is not intended to be considered in isolation or as a substitute for the financial information prepared and presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States of America ("U.S. GAAP"). The Company defines non-GAAP financial measures by excluding the impact of share-based compensation expenses and credit-related impairment/(reversal) of long-term investments from the respective GAAP financial measures. The Company presents the non-GAAP financial measures because they are used by the management to evaluate its operating performance and formulate business plans. The Company also believes that the use of the non-GAAP financial measures facilitates investors' assessment of its operating performance.

Non-GAAP financial measures are not defined under U.S. GAAP and are not presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Non-GAAP financial measures have limitations as analytical tools. One of the key limitations of using the aforementioned non-GAAP financial measures is that they do not reflect all items of expenses that affect the Firm's operations. Share-based compensation expenses and credit-related impairment/(reversal) of long-term investments have been and may continue to be incurred in the business and are not reflected in the presentation of non-GAAP measures. Further, the non-GAAP financial measures may differ from the non-GAAP information used by other companies, including peer companies, and therefore their comparability may be limited. The Company compensates for these limitations by reconciling the non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable U.S. GAAP measures, all of which should be considered when evaluating the Company's performance. The Company encourages you to review its financial information in its entirety and not rely on a single financial measure.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the listing comes as Anthropic, the tech giant behind the popular AI chatbot Claude, officially made its much-anticipated stock market debut on Thursday, Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that as per the latest X post from Coinbase, the exchange confirmed the availability of Anthropic (ANT) shares for eligible users in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that leading cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has confirmed the official listing of artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic (ANT) shares on its trading platform in the U.S. and U.K.

According to recent reports, the listing comes as Anthropic, the tech giant behind the popular AI chatbot Claude, officially made its much-anticipated stock market debut on Thursday, Nov. 19, with its shares seeing massive volatility.

Recent findings suggest that as per the latest X post from Coinbase, the exchange confirmed the availability of Anthropic (ANT) shares for eligible users in the U.S. and U.K.

It's notable to mention that ANT isn't a cryptocurrency but a traditional stock. Coinbase's support for ANT shares indicates the firm's efforts to expand its offerings beyond crypto into traditional financial markets.

Anthropic has set a newly introduced historic precedent, having successfully raised about $81 billion in its initial public offering (IPO). This is the biggest IPO ever.

The artificial intelligence company sold 980 million shares at $83 per share, significantly higher than its previously unveiled price range of $70 to $78.

This brought Anthropic's initial valuation to about $1.5 trillion, making the tech giant one of the most valuable publicly listed firms in the world right from the get-go.

But as Anthropic shares started trading on the Nasdaq exchange, the ANT ticker saw massive volatility.

It has been revealed that as per Reuters, Anthropic shares began trading at $111.50. This represented an enormous 34% premium over the IPO price.

At the initial peak, Anthropic's market cap exceeded $2 trillion, surpassing SpaceX's valuation when it debuted on the market in June.

Industry observers note that anthropic shares slipped to around $95 as the stock gave back a significant chunk of its gains. This was partly due to investors looking to book their profits.

Nonetheless, Anthropic shares were still trading comfortably above their $83 IPO price.

The volatility surrounding Anthropic's stock market debut signals increasing doubts about the AI investment craze.

The listing of Anthropic shares is just one of Coinbase's moves to enter traditional financial markets.

Instead of just providing cryptocurrency trading, the exchange is looking to become a platform for multiple asset classes.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Coinbase had already listed Anthropic pre-IPO perpetual futures for eligible non-U.S. people on Nov. 18.

The perpetual futures were derivative contracts that allowed traders to speculate on Anthropic's valuation before its shares officially started trading on Nasdaq.

In a recent development, with the latest listing, eligible Coinbase owners in the U.S. and U.K. can now trade the publicly listed Anthropic shares.

Anthropic's blockbuster debut comes as financial markets have been rocked by recent volatility, with tech stocks and crypto facing selling pressure.

NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO indicates

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • It has been revealed that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

It has been revealed that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO mentioned he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint mentioned he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

White also allegedly stated that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or blueprint.”.

Industry observers note that pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also stated the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Recent findings suggest that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

It has been revealed that pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears stated the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

It has been revealed that “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” noted David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Industry observers note that pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

Mortgage headlines aren’t as big a concern as your cost per closing

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027.
  • It has been revealed that I understand why it spread.
  • It has been revealed that the Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027.

It has been revealed that I understand why it spread. Freddie Mac had the 30-year fixed at 7.28% on Oct. 1, up from 6.01% in February and the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. If everything moves the wrong way at once, 9% could sound possible.

It has been revealed that the Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments. It is likely causing some anxiety for many agents.

According to recent reports, it helps to look at what it would actually take. Cotality’s chief economist, Selma Hepp, raised 9% on CNBC as a worst case, not a forecast. HousingWire’s Logan Mohtashami laid out the math: the 10-year would have to push past 6%, and mortgage spreads would have to widen well beyond the roughly 2% they sit at today. That requires a hot economy, oil prices that stay high and a Fed that keeps hiking past what markets expect, all lasting well into next year. September’s jobs report showed 29,000 new jobs, which already works against the hot-economy part.

Recent findings suggest that so I wouldn’t initiative around 9%. I also wouldn’t plan around rates falling back to 6% anytime soon. The Fed’s own projections show no cuts in 2027, and the Mortgage Bankers Association expects rates to stay close to where they are.

A crash needs forced sellers, and we don’t have many. Homeowners with a mortgage carry an average loan-to-value of about 44%, and only around 2% are underwater, according to Cotality. That isn’t 2008.

Sources indicate that what we do have is fewer deals. In early October, pending sales were about 10% less than the year before, and purchase applications were down 14%. Those applications turn into closings 30 to 90 days later, so a lot of teams have been looking at a softer first quarter. At today’s rate, the payment that covered a $400,000 loan in February covers about $357,000 now. Same buyer, same budget, about 11% less loan.

It has been revealed that prices mostly hold, and the deal count shrinks. I think of 2027 as a consolidation year rather than a crash year.

In August, I wrote here that cost-per-lead is the wrong number to run a team on, and that cost-per-closed deal is the one that tells you the truth. A slow year is when that stops being a philosophy and turns into a real potential problem.

Most of what a team spends to generate business is fixed. The ad campaign, vendor contracts, the ISA hours and the coaching all get billed whether deals close or not. When conversion falls, none of those invoices get smaller.

Say a team spends $6,000 a month on lead generation and closes 12 deals a quarter from it. That’s $1,500 per closing. Then buyer conversion slips, and the same spend produces nine closings. Now each closing costs $2,000. Nothing on the invoice changed, and every deal got a third more expensive.

That’s the exposure I’d worry about: a cost structure built for a 6.5% market, running in a 7.5% one.

The gap between a team that knows its number and one that doesn’t gets much wider when volume drops.

You can’t control the 10-year Treasury. These are the things you can control though:.

Find your cost per closing by source. Add up everything you spend on each lead source, including ad spend, platform and referral fees, ISA time and software, and divide it by the closed transactions that source produced over the last 12 months. Use closings, not appointments or signed agreements. Most team leads I talk to have never broken this out by source, and the answer usually surprises them.

According to recent reports, stress-test it at a lower deal count. Run the same numbers assuming 20% fewer closings. Any source that ends up costing more per closing than your net is one to fix or cut now, while you still have room to choose.

In a recent development, shift your mix toward sellers and your sphere. Buyers are the first to stall when rates jump. Sellers still have to move for fresh jobs, divorces, estates, and growing families, whatever the rate happens to be, and your past clients are sitting on real equity. If most of your pipeline is buyer leads, 2027 will hurt more than it should.

Lengthen your nurture instead of cutting it. The buyer who is priced out at 7.5% may be ready at 6.75%. If your follow-up ends at 90 days, someone else gets that deal if rates turn, and you end up paying for the same lead twice.

It has been revealed that give your agents training so they can handle these clients. Don’t promise rates will fall. Understand the concern first, then help the buyer evaluate actual numbers without treating a forecast as a fact.

2023 had the fewest existing-home sales since 1995. The teams I watched hold up through it weren’t the ones that guessed right about rates. They were the ones that knew what each closing cost them and kept moving money toward what was working.

There will be another very scary hot topic after this one, and another after that. The best hedge against all of them is the same: know your cost per closing, and build a pipeline that doesn’t depend on buyers feeling good about rates.

Robyn Thompson DeSantos is the founder and CEO of Ascension Group, a business solutions and management firm for real estate team leaders and brokers.

FHA’s reverse mortgage book faces headwinds from home prices, fewer payoffs

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Housing Administration’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress states the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year.
  • 16, found that the MMI Fund’s overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept.
  • Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Housing Administration’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress states the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year.

The report, released Nov. 16, found that the MMI Fund’s overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept. 30, moving from 11.47% last year to 10.29% this year. The current figure, however, is roughly five times higher than fund’s statutory minimum requirement of 2%.

Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026. The FHA attributed this decline mainly to macroeconomic dynamics and program-specific cash flows.

The reverse mortgage portfolio, which accounts for less than 4% of the fund’s insurance in force, is “much more sensitive to home prices,” the report explained. Slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts have increased projected losses for the HECM program. In addition, loan payoffs — which represent more favorable recovery outcomes than other disposition methods like foreclosures — have become less common and have pushed losses higher.

The agency also noted that the HECM program “spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.” These claims, which are generated when FHA acquires loans that hit the 98% maximum claim amount threshold, are a known driver of volatility in the HECM book. They remain a key cost to monitor for reverse mortgage issuers and servicers.

While the federally insured reverse mortgage portfolio is still in the black, the takeaway from the report is that its capital support can change rapidly due to shifts in home price appreciation, payoff behaviors and the frequency of assignment claims. These factors drive FHA policy decisions, as well as Ginnie Mae execution in the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) market.

The report illustrates that FHA-insured options remain central to the wider reverse mortgage market, even as volumes edge lower. In FY 2026, FHA insured 24,162 HECMs representing a maximum claim amount (MCA) of $12.81 billion.

Endorsements were down about 14% from the 28,149 HECMs endorsed in FY 2025. MCA volume also fell from about $15.5 billion in 2025 to roughly $13.5 billion in 2026.

In a recent development, but even with that pullback, the HECM program “remains a large part of the market,” according to the report. Historic data reinforces the sector’s structural shift. HECM endorsements peaked above 110,000 in 2009 with roughly $30.5 billion in MCA. Volumes have trended lower for more than a decade, with visible rebounds in 2020–2022 during a period of low interest rates and high home price growth. But higher rates and slower price growth since 2023 have softened demand.

Industry observers note that to fill the gap, lenders are focusing on proprietary reverse mortgages through their retail, wholesale and correspondent channels. The wider availability of these products has propelled a shift in market share as private-label loans accounted for more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September, according to New View Advisors.

“I think that product diversity is great because we’re able to serve more clients that the FHA product wouldn’t handle,” Jesse Allen, president of 55+ lending at Rate, told HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD) at this month’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo.

He said these may be “mass affluent clients who have home values of $2 million or $3 million, and they really want to tap their equity without the debt service to achieve their goals,” but they can also be clients who don’t fit the HECM qualification requirements and are using reverse mortgage proceeds to consolidate debt.

According to recent reports, “This is another regulatory guideline NRMLA has advocated for. ‘Hey, we’re paying off consumer debts. Let’s not count that toward the the qualification process.’ Proprietary allows us to do that and HECM does not,” Allen noted.

In a recent development, FHA’s FY 2026 report includes a dedicated HECM chapter that details borrower profiles and loan features. These include HECM loan purposes (such as home purchases versus refinancing of existing debt), payment plan options, interest rate types, borrower ages and maximum claim amounts and initial draws by recent borrower cohorts.

The agency emphasizes that its actuaries model HECM cash flows separately from forward mortgages and explicitly stress-test the reverse portfolio under varying home price appreciation scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that home price appreciation assumptions affect multiple levers across the program — including the available equity at the end of the loan, the size of recoveries through property sales and the loss severity tied to claims. Indirectly, home price growth can also impact payoff incentives.

Sources indicate that the report notes that waning price growth in 2026 had an “outsized negative impact” on HECM capital compared with forward mortgages. This underscores why even modest regional or national home price corrections are more consequential for HMBS investors and issuers than for traditional mortgage-backed securities.

Industry observers note that the stand-alone capital ratio of 5.43% for the HECM portfolio suggests that FHA still has room to absorb stress, but far less cushion than in the prior three years when the ratio ranged between roughly 16% and 25%. It also may create more difficulty for industry advocates in their push to reduce upfront mortgage insurance premiums.

According to recent reports, in September, Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley told RMD that the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with the current mortgage insurance structure for FHA single-family loans and reverse mortgages. Gormley’s comments prompted pushback from NRMLA, which said it would continue to “dialogue with them around more risk-based pricing.”.

An industry professional who was granted anonymity was more blunt in calling for lower premiums.

“The reality is this, if a client has to pay 2% to obtain the right to draw up to 30% of their home’s value, they will seek out other options,” the source said. “It should come as no surprise that HEIs and HEAs have been popping up everywhere. Even the gains on the proprietary side are the result of FHA’s inaction. Clients would rather accrue 10% interest annually to a lender than pay 2% upfront to a government insurer.”.

The FHA report’s policy section does not identify any major upcoming structural changes to the HECM program, but it does highlight several items of operational relevance.

This includes contract funding reallocation for assigned HECM property preservation expenses. FHA mentions a reallocation of contract funding tied to property preservation on assigned HECM collateral. While it’s a technical issue, it could affect vendors and servicers who manage preservation and conveyance on properties with HECM balances that are acquired by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

According to recent reports, fraud detection, data analytics and remediation were also mentioned. These areas are not limited to the HECM portfolio and apply across FHA single-family programs. Given the growing population of senior borrowers and the history of consumer protection scrutiny for reverse mortgages, these efforts may lead to tighter oversight of origination practices and borrower counseling outcomes in the HECM channel.

It has been revealed that FHA also discussed ongoing system modernization efforts, including those tied to FHA Catalyst modules and uniform appraisal data initiatives. Over time, the report explained, better data capturing should improve the accuracy of HECM-backed property valuations — a key driver of assignment timing and loss estimates — and could result in more precise disclosures for HMBS investors.

The report also placed attention on the new permanent loss-mitigation waterfall for FHA forward mortgages that went into effect at the end of 2025. While that waterfall does not directly apply to HECMs, it signals a broader effort by the agency to standardize workout options and reduce cycles of repeated defaults. This approach could inform any future redesign of default resolution frameworks for reverse mortgages.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

According to recent reports, sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

According to recent reports, paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Recent findings suggest that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers stated they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In a recent development, in its own analysis, The Latest York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

According to recent reports, “I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.
