AI agent provider Sierra closes $1.75B investment amid rapid revenue growth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Six months after its last funding round, artificial intelligence startup Sierra Technologies Inc.
  • Recent findings suggest that greenoaks and Lightspeed led the Series F deal.
  • According to recent reports, sierra sells a set of cloud services that enables workers to create AI agents without writing code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:49 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Six months after its last funding round, artificial intelligence startup Sierra Technologies Inc. today revealed that it has closed a $1.75 billion late-stage investment.

Recent findings suggest that greenoaks and Lightspeed led the Series F deal. They were joined by a group of returning backers that included Alphabet Inc.’s GV fund.

According to recent reports, sierra sells a set of cloud services that enables workers to create AI agents without writing code. The centerpiece of the suite is Ghostwriter, which can automatically generate agents based on user-provided prompts and files. A software team, for example, could upload a set of bug reports and request an agent that can automatically group them by problem type.

Recent findings suggest that ghostwriter checks the dataset that consumers upload for formatting errors before putting it to use. Once an agent is ready, the tool simulates user conversations to find potential bugs. Ghostwriter places particular emphasis on edge cases, unusual requests that can trip up an agent if they’re not addressed during development.

According to recent reports, sierra also offers a second development tool called Horizon. It can be used to create agents that automate time-consuming tasks. A marketing team could build an agent that monitors user interactions with a product page over several months, finds areas for improvement and automatically makes the necessary optimizations.

Sierra powers customers’ agents using more than a dozen large language models. Simple requests are sent to latency-optimized LLMs, while more complex queries are processed by pricier frontier models. Sierra states that it also uses several internally developed algorithms.

According to recent reports, customers can manage their AI projects using a third Sierra product called Agent Studio. According to the tech giant, it includes over 40 connectors that enable agents to retrieve information from external systems. There’s also a tool for building custom connectors.

Recent findings suggest that agent Studio detects gaps in agents’ knowledge. Furthermore, it can automatically fix some of those gaps. The platform detects when a human support representative answers a customer inquiry that the help desk hasn’t encountered before and turns it into a knowledge base article. From there, agents can use the article to answer similar requests.

The studio also lends itself to certain other tasks. A collaboration feature enables multiple team members to review agent updates before they roll out to production. If a technical issue makes it past the review, developers can use a debugging tool to study what went wrong. The tool displays every single step of the workflow through which an agent processes prompts.

In a recent development, rounding out Sierra’s product portfolio is an AI assistant called Explorer. It can proactively flag notable business events without a prompt and search through a manufacturer’s internal datasets. In some cases, it also generates business advice.

Sierra’s latest raise, its third in 14 months, comes a few weeks after its annualized revenue topped $400 million. The company disclosed at the time that it had added nearly half the sum over the preceding quarter. Its customer base now includes half the Fortune 50.

Sierra will reportedly use the new funding to enhance its product portfolio and hire more salespeople.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that by many estimations, real estate professionals are facing the most challenging housing market in recent memory in 2027. Unlike in the past, many will be doing so with access to more resources than ever designed to ensure they are feeling healthy, at the peak of their game and ready to tackle whatever the 2027 housing market throws at them.

This is because over the past year, several brokerages announced a variety of wellness programs and health insurance opportunities they are now offering to agents, who as independent contractors, typically do not have access to things like insurance through their brokerage.

Since the start of 2026, ENRG Realty, Compass International Holdings, Equity Union Real Estate and John R. Wood Properties have revealed the launch of health insurance or wellness benefits initiatives.

In a recent development, “We were founded on Maslow Hierarchy of Needs, so health insurance fits right in with some of the core basic values that we need to provide to our agents so they can be successful and thrive,” Erinn Nobel, the co-founder and president of ENRG Realty and a HousingWire Woman of Influence award winner, said. “In order for our agents to function at a high level, they can’t be sitting at home worried about an illness or being able to pay their bills because they don’t have health coverage. It is a foundational offering and a benefit for us to be able to provide it for our agents.”.

Nobel said that while some Realtor boards or associations offer health insurance, there is often just one policy option, something she experienced first hand after moving to Alaska from Washington state.

It has been revealed that “It was great to be able to access insurance through our board, but there was only one initiative, so you couldn’t shop around,” Nobel remarked. “It just didn’t sit well with me that my options were so limited.”.

A similar experience with challenges accessing insurance for his family is also what inspired Harma Hartouni, the CEO of Equity Union Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, to begin providing his agents with access to group-style health coverage options, including a nationwide PPO network, through a partnership with Trident BPO.

When he approached the executive team about launching this initiative, Hartouni remarked they were a bit divided as to whether or not they should do this.

“Some thought the agents wouldn’t care, but some of our managers thought it was great,” Hartouni remarked. “Ultimately, our agents are our clients, and I knew that if these people were not healthy or not in a clear mindset in this challenging market, they would not function well.”.

In the current uncertain economic environment, Hartouni added that the offering has also provided many agents, who previously had access to insurance through a spouse who lost their job, a level of peace of mind that they couldn’t previously provide.

“The consistent feedback from agents is that they are saving money and are able to see better doctors,” Hartouni said.

Nobel remarked she’s heard similar feedback from her agents. After rolling out the program, Nobel said she and her team received countless messages from agents saying thank you. Beyond better serving existing agents, Nobel said the program also helped ENRG Realty with agent recruitment.

“It has become an attraction magnet for us. Savvy agents that have been in the industry for a while are starting to really compare brokerages and look at what benefits they get from each brokerage and the different values they provide,” Nobel remarked. “If an agent already has access to health insurance through a spouse or partner, then this may not convey the same value as it would to a self-employed single mom who would love to have access to health care.”.

Hartouni has also noticed the agent recruitment benefits of offering health insurance.

According to recent reports, “The smart broker is looking for producing agents that are in the middle of their career, where they still have plenty of years left in the business to learn and grow, but have already begun to establish themselves,” he said. “But these agents often have families to think about and how can we help them have one less thing to worry about? We can provide them with access to health insurance.”.

While John R. Wood Properties is not providing agents with access to health insurance, the brokerage recently confirmed it was providing its agents with access to individualized coaching focused on their personal well-being and professional development, through a partnership with HatchPath. Through the program, agents can gain access to coaching support across a wide range of areas including nutrition, stress management, mental resilience, leadership, career development and major life transitions.

Recent findings suggest that “People are just so burn[ed] out in general and everybody is on edge from personal challenges, financial challenges, family challenges. I just thought what better way to support our people than to give them access to coaching,” Corey McCloskey, the president of John R. Wood Properties, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think a lot of us who run businesses have realized that you bring your whole self to work. You can’t just turn off what’s happening in your personal life when you walk into your office — it affects you whether you realize it or not.”.

While still in the early stages of the rollout, McCloskey remarked she has seen her agents and staff use HatchPath coaching for help with everything from financial planning to fitness and overall physical wellness.

Although brokerages are continuing to face challenging housing market conditions and ever-tightening profit margins, these executives believe it’s crucial for brokerages to support their agents beyond just professional development.

It has been revealed that “If we are encouraging people to be entrepreneurs, we have to support them and provide them some sort of value,” Nobel remarked. “Anytime we can offer a benefit that has real value to agents, we really look to do that because ultimately that is what we as a brokerage are supposed to do — provide value for our agents.”.

Nobel added that she would encourage more brokerages to consider providing agents with access to health insurance.

Industry observers note that “This is something that we need to be offering our agents in the world right now,” she said. “Offering insurance is what is best for our industry.”.

McCloskey, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, shares a similar view.

Recent findings suggest that “Knowing that not only us, but other companies are supporting agents as whole people, I think that will only serve to make our industry better,” she stated. “The younger leaders coming into the industry have seen the toll this industry can take on someone who doesn’t take care of themselves. They want to do things differently, and I think we have an opportunity now that we’ve never had before where we can offer these sorts of things to people and really tell them how important they are to us.”.

Veteran commodity trader Peter Brandt has provided yet another bearish outlook for the world's largest cryptocurrency, arguing that the crypto asset could see much more misery if its historical market trends play out.

Bitcoin Bitcoin Every bull market phase in BTC's history has ended with at least a 75% correction of the previous parabolic bull trend. Could this be what's happening in Bitcoin? https://t.co/PVXJpetSyO.

Brandt's latest doomsday prediction comes at a time when Bitcoin is still trying to recover from its biggest sell-off to date, which has wiped out close to half of its market value from its October 2025 peak.

The trader's latest post on X highlights a pattern he has found throughout Bitcoin's price history: previous bull runs have always ended with devastating market corrections.

"Every bull market phase in the history of BTC has ended with at least a 75% correction of the prior parabolic bull trend," Brandt's X post reads.

Continuing his warning, Brandt raised an alarming question: "Is this what is happening with Bitcoin?".

The trading veteran has not put a number on the possible crash. But his words point toward the possibility that the current drop in Bitcoin might be part of a larger correction and not just a temporary dip.

A look at Bitcoin's historical crashes could paint a scary picture.

Bitcoin has a history of sharp corrections following major bull runs.

For example, the crypto asset dropped by around 84% from its December 2017 high to its December 2018 low. Another example of such a deep price correction can be found in the 2022 bear market, when BTC saw a drop of around 77% from its November 2021 all-time high.

These historic crashes have shown the extreme losses that Bitcoin investors have faced during such market corrections.

According to recent reports, at the time of writing on Nov. 20, Bitcoin is currently trading at around $62,000, which is almost 51% below its October 2025 all-time high.

If it were to undergo a 75% price correction from its all-time high, then it would drop to around $31,550.

But it's worth mentioning that Brandt referred to a correction of the prior parabolic bull trend, which may not be the same as a 75% correction from the peak.

Interestingly enough, this is not the first time the trader has warned about an even darker future for Bitcoin's price.

Sources indicate that earlier, on Nov. 15, Brandt shared a weekly BTC chart showing a potential head-and-shoulders formation, a technical pattern that usually signals a bearish reversal.

According to Brandt, if the pattern is confirmed, there's a chance that Bitcoin could never revisit its previous all-time high in his lifetime.

Sources indicate that the chart he shared also indicates an key zone between $60,000 and $65,000. A confirmed breakdown below this zone could further strengthen the bearish outlook.

In a recent development, moreover, there is still plenty of selling pressure in the crypto market. The latest patch from Lookonchain on Nov. 19 revealed that U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had seen net outflows of around $975 million over the past seven days. The biggest net outflows came from BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT).

  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the organization’s experimental arm, declared the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith stated on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Industry observers note that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Customers cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of customers. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

Bitcoin (BTC) is facing renewed selling pressure as large holders continue to reduce their exposure, with on-chain data showing that whales have redistributed about $3.4 billion worth of the cryptocurrency over the past two weeks.

Sources indicate that notably, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has fallen nearly 13% over the past week. The decline extends its November losses, bringing its price to a three-month low.

According to analyst Ali Martinez, large entities have sold or redistributed 48,618 BTC, valued at approximately $3.4 billion, over the past two weeks.

“Whales are still reducing their exposure. The selling hasn’t stopped yet,” Martinez tweeted.

The continued distribution suggests that major holders are yet to regain confidence in Bitcoin’s near-term prospects. With thousands of coins changing hands, the market faces the challenge of absorbing this supply without triggering further downward pressure.

Beyond whale activity, Bitcoin’s weekly performance is adding to concerns about the market’s strength.

Analyst Ted Pillows noted that the cryptocurrency has closed six consecutive weeks in the red, a pattern previously seen during bear markets. Trading below both moving averages further weakens its recovery prospects.

“Along with that, Bitcoin failed to hold both the 200W EMA and 200W MA, which is a major sign of weakness. As long as BTC stays below these levels, sellers are in full control,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, several vital price levels have given way, leaving Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline.

Mookie, an advocate at Bitget Wallet and ambassador at Dinari Global, highlighted the cryptocurrency’s failure to maintain successive support levels, warning that $57,700 could come into focus if buyers fail to regain control.

“If BTC can’t get back above $66.5K. we could see another drop toward the July low at $57.7K. But if buyers push it back above $66.5K we might finally see a bounce. Still not convinced we’re done dropping,” he noted.

Industry observers note that his comments put $66,500 at the center of Bitcoin’s immediate price outlook. Reclaiming that level could help buyers regain some momentum, while another rejection would leave the July low of $57,700 as a potential downside target.

Despite the prevailing bearish sentiment, some market observers believe Bitcoin could be approaching a turning point.

Gordon, founder of Crypto Crib and co-founder of Alphametrics, pointed to a potential inverse head-and-shoulders formation, suggesting that extreme pessimism could set the stage for a reversal.

According to recent reports, “All longs have been wiped out, sentiment is max bearish, and retail is going heavy short. This is where reversal happens,” he commented.

In a recent development, an inverse head-and-shoulders pattern is a technical formation often associated with a potential bullish reversal after an extended decline. It typically consists of three troughs, with the middle one forming the lowest point.

Sources indicate that gordon’s assessment offers a contrasting view to the warnings from other analysts. He believes that widespread bearish positioning and the liquidation of leveraged long positions could create conditions for buyers to return.

However, the formation does not guarantee an immediate recovery. Bitcoin still needs enough buying interest to reverse its recent losses and reclaim key price levels.

At press time, BTC was trading at $59,299, down 5.40% over the past 24 hours.

Cost cutting is not cost reduction; builders and trades face a test

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A reliable estimate of the tariff burden on a typical newly built American home puts the cost at $12,919, or about $4.88 per square foot.
  • That is before accounting for broader inflation in construction labor, transportation, services and other inputs that homebuilders must absorb while trying to make their homes affordable to increasingly price-sensitive customers.
  • According to recent reports, this informed baseline calculation of tariff impact at the fresh-home level, developed by homebuilding supply-chain consultancy Strategem through its Strategy Pulse Pro platform, updates the National Association of Home Builders‘ April 2025 builder-reported tariff-cost estimate of $10,900 to reflect subsequent trade-policy changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A reliable estimate of the tariff burden on a typical newly built American home puts the cost at $12,919, or about $4.88 per square foot.

That is before accounting for broader inflation in construction labor, transportation, services and other inputs that homebuilders must absorb while trying to make their homes affordable to increasingly price-sensitive customers.

According to recent reports, this informed baseline calculation of tariff impact at the fresh-home level, developed by homebuilding supply-chain consultancy Strategem through its Strategy Pulse Pro platform, updates the National Association of Home Builders‘ April 2025 builder-reported tariff-cost estimate of $10,900 to reflect subsequent trade-policy changes. The model distributes tariff exposure across 17 material categories, with hardware and fasteners, steel products, lumber, cabinets, windows and aluminum accounting for some of the highest estimated costs.

By its nature, Strategem’s tally is a modeled cost burden, not a direct measure of tariffs paid on every home or of the amount passed through to buyers.

It has been revealed that still, it illustrates a difficult dilemma for homebuilders, and one none of them can simply avoid: Costs imposed upstream cannot necessarily be recovered downstream. And in that downstream market, households increasingly lack the financial capacity or confidence to buy homes at the prices builders need to charge.

That predicament, predictable in a falling market, is a reflexive homebuilding firm response that reverberates through homebuilding’s wider ecosystem like a bad-trip flashback. Homebuilders are looking to their suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and trade contractors to shoulder more of the financial pain.

It’s a law of dismal science physics during a downturn: Wringing a bit of margin improvement by most builders means squeezing suppliers’ margins into further negative territory.

In a recent development, the danger is that some builders may, and often do, push their business partners beyond what they can reasonably absorb. This tactic, seductive as it may seem as a way to claw back input cost reductions, mostly serves as a temporary fix. Ultimately, such quick fixes undermine the very production capacity, service reliability, and competitive supplier pools they will need to survive the downturn and recover.

Homebuilders have spent much of the past two years using price reductions, mortgage-rate buydowns and other incentives to preserve sales velocity. Those concessions have helped sustain production, but they have also eroded the earnings cushion – the “shock absorber” – that previously allowed many builders to absorb rising costs without substantially disrupting operations.

The squeeze is occurring on both sides of builders’ income statements. According to NAHB’s November 13 analysis of Producer Price Index data, goods used in newly introduced residential construction rose 9.8% year over year in October, while service inputs increased 11.3%. The combined input index rose 10.4%, including a 5.8% increase in building-material prices.

Industry observers note that these are input-price indexes, not equivalent percentage increases in the total cost of constructing a house. Still, they reveal why slowing demand has not delivered the broad-based cost relief builders might otherwise expect.

The pressure is particularly difficult for smaller builders and suppliers with limited financial reserves. They must keep enough business flowing to cover fixed costs while protecting the margins and working capital required to remain viable.

Ken Pinto, a longtime homebuilding strategic-sourcing executive and co-founder of Strategem, and a friend of The Builder’s Daily, believes the industry risks conflating two fundamentally different types of cost reduction.

Purchasing departments are reporting savings from increasingly competitive bidding, he says, but those reductions often come from suppliers sacrificing profitability rather than from lasting improvements in how homes are built.

“When you reduce costs by going out to bid, going out to bid, going out to bid, you’re not taking cost out of the supply chain; you’re taking margins out,” Pinto notes.

This self-preservatory instinct among homebuilding business decision-makers has important, potentially risky, consequences. A trade contractor who accepts a lower price to keep crews working may provide immediate relief to a builder’s direct costs, but the underlying costs of labor, transportation, insurance, equipment, and materials may remain unchanged.

When demand eventually recovers, those concessions may disappear. More troubling, some suppliers may not survive long enough to participate in the recovery.

Pinto points to manufacturers facing higher costs for steel, copper and resin-based products while struggling to secure corresponding price increases. Their customers may be able to delay accepting price increases, but the underlying costs do not disappear simply because builders refuse to pay them. The resulting margin compression can become unsustainable.

Conversations with homebuilding purchasing professionals suggest that the opportunities for further reductions vary considerably by category. Some material suppliers remain willing to compete aggressively for market share, particularly in areas where slower construction activity has created excess capacity. But trade contractors face different circumstances.

Industry observers note that years of declining production volume have already weakened some local subcontractor businesses. In some markets, established trade firms have closed, while others struggle with cash flow, payment disputes and mechanics’ liens.

At the same time, immigration enforcement has reduced labor availability in trades including framing, concrete, masonry, roofing, electrical work and painting. The result is an increasingly uneven marketplace in which a builder may find materials readily available but struggle to secure the skilled labor required to install them.

Residential construction also faces growing competition for certain resources from the extraordinary investment flowing into artificial intelligence infrastructure and data-center construction.

That competition is particularly acute in markets where large commercial projects – especially of note in Texas and Virginia ­– require concrete, electrical equipment, transportation capacity and specialized labor. Although residential and data-center construction workforces are not interchangeable, competition for certain services and materials can raise costs even as homebuilding activity slows.

The risk extends into 2027. A contractor with too little work today may be unable to retain skilled crews until demand improves. A builder who pushes that contractor’s prices below sustainable levels may find the contractor has disappeared, downsized, or committed its remaining capacity elsewhere when upcoming-home orders return.

According to recent reports, that is not merely a supplier problem. It becomes a builder’s problem across the construction cycle, quality, customer service, and profitability.

Pinto argues that builders and trade contractors have a much larger opportunity to improve profitability by jointly addressing avoidable operating costs.

Industry observers note that one recurring example is construction scheduling. When a subcontractor arrives at a jobsite that is not ready, the contractor incurs labor, transportation and administrative costs without productive work. Unreliable schedules make it harder to allocate crews, while late changes, rework and unnecessary return visits consume resources neither party can afford to waste.

Industry observers note that “We still get subcontractors showing up to job sites, and the job’s not ready for them. So, a dry run. This shouldn’t be happening,” Pinto claims.

Consider the contrasting approach between 1. a homebuilder demanding a 5% reduction in a trade contractor’s bid and 2. the two businesses collaborating to eliminate repeated crew mobilizations, incomplete jobsite preparation and avoidable rework.

Industry observers note that the first approach may reduce the builder’s invoice while leaving the contractor’s expenses unchanged. The second can reduce the actual cost of completing the work, creating room for both companies to improve their economics.

Achieving these operational efficiencies becomes especially important when homebuilding’s lower production volumes should give operating teams more opportunity to coordinate schedules, standardize specifications and eliminate recurring inefficiencies.

Sources indicate that pinto is developing a collaborative workshop, Tearing Down the Walls, with former subcontractor and Builderbeast Consulting founder Don Bronchick and industry colleague Andrew Stevens. The workshop’s premise is that builders and trade contractors can improve their economics by jointly examining the processes that create unnecessary costs.

Sources indicate that the approach requires both parties to share information, acknowledge their contributions to inefficiency, and agree on measurable improvements. That is more demanding than threatening to award a contract to the lowest bidder, but it offers the possibility of savings that endure through a market recovery.

In a recent development, homebuilding’s consolidation wave adds another dimension to the challenge. Larger builders have gained substantial purchasing leverage, but their long-term returns increasingly depend on integrating local operating expertise, supplier relationships and construction capabilities to build more effective enterprises.

It has been revealed that the purchasing organization offering the lowest quoted prices does not necessarily lead to the lowest completed-home costs. A supplier who consistently meets schedules, maintains qualified crews, resolves field problems swiftly, and supports a builder through fluctuations in demand may be worth more than the nominal difference between competing bids.

It has been revealed that that does not excuse poor performance or prevent builders from replacing suppliers who cannot meet reasonable cost, quality, or service requirements. Competitive bidding remains necessary, and some vendors may still have room to lower their prices.

The key question is whether builders understand and choose between extracting a concession and improving the economics of the entire production process.

Industry observers note that for 2027, the choice to improve holistic economics should guide purchasing and operating decisions. Builders need to understand which costs suppliers can control, which are driven by external forces, and which stem from the builder’s own practices. They also need to evaluate suppliers’ financial health, preserve alternative sources of capacity where practical, and measure total installed costs rather than purchase prices alone.

These measures will not close the affordability gap or restore lost homebuyer demand. Nor can they fully offset tariffs, higher financing costs, or skilled-worker shortages. They can, however, prevent homebuilders from worsening their operating position while trying to protect near-term margins.

Homebuilding companies have every reason to ask their business partners to share the burden of a difficult market. But there is a meaningful difference between sharing that burden and transferring it to a partner with no capacity to absorb it. Business leaders know the difference.

They know the ones best positioned for recovery may not be those that extract the deepest concessions today. They know that the real, more structural solution – and one that should keep most valued partner relationships intact – reduces the actual cost of producing homes while preserving the trust and transparency, skills and productive capacity that will allow them to build profitably when customers return.

That’s not to say it’s the easier, softer way forward, but when demand finally strengthens, a homebuilder will need more than an order backlog and available lots. That team will need capable partners still willing – and able – to build the homes. And they know it.

  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • In a recent development, the startup stated today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

In a recent development, the startup stated today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really major step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

According to recent reports, nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles noted.

It has been revealed that boles stated the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles remarked. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

According to recent reports, retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “crucial step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson mentioned in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

In a recent development, the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The firm is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The manufacturer has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#156308. Raleigh’s housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds

Raleigh’s housing reforms helped ease rents, Pew study finds

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing.
  • Sources indicate that following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found.
  • The report highlights how adding newly introduced housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for years, homebuilding leaders have argued that the most effective way to lower housing costs is to build more, and that cities that adopt pro-housing reforms will be rewarded with greater supply and more attainable housing. New research from The Pew Charitable Trusts shows what happened when Raleigh, N.C., followed that playbook.

Sources indicate that following the pandemic, Raleigh overhauled its zoning and land use laws to make building easier, Pew found. The result was a building boom, particularly for the townhomes and apartments the city’s earlier rules constrained. This uptick in homebuilding made renting more affordable in North Carolina’s capital city, especially for middle-income households and younger residents.

The report highlights how adding newly introduced housing supply at scale can improve housing affordability, echoing similar impacts that followed concerted rezoning efforts in Minneapolis-St. Paul, Minn., and Austin, Texas. The same dynamic is playing out across the Sun Belt, where many of the nation’s fastest-growing metros also have some of the loosest zoning rules, and where rents and home prices have dropped more dramatically than anywhere else in the country.

Raleigh didn’t rely on a single fix to make building housing easier. Its reforms combined a rewrite of its form-based code, an end to parking minimums, denser building near transit and a housing bond to support affordable housing.

“Of all of the drivers of housing costs – population growth, an influx of high-income earners, high land costs and high construction costs – we have the most agency and direct control over restrictive zoning regulations,” Patrick Young, Raleigh’s planning and development director, remarked in a statement.

Raleigh’s 2021 zoning reform, which expanded the city’s already-established form-based code, opened the door to more “missing middle” housing. It did so by replacing units-per-acre caps with physical standards such as lot size, yards, and building height.

The changes legalized duplexes, triplexes and quadplexes in more residential districts and expanded where townhomes can be built. Under the latest form-based code, further refined in 2022, builders can now construct small apartment buildings and tiny houses with up to two dwelling units on compact infill lots.

As a result, builders can now construct missing middle housing in more of Raleigh’s neighborhoods, a shift that Pew links to better affordability for middle-income and younger residents.

Recent findings suggest that raleigh eliminated its citywide parking minimums in 2022. That allowed developers to fit more housing units on each property and, in some cases, spared them the expense of building costly parking structures, which can often make a project too costly to pursue.

According to recent reports, the city also spurred housing growth by allowing taller, denser buildings near major transit corridors. Transit Overlay District zones allowed for an extra story along Bus Rapid Transit corridors, extending half a mile along some local bus routes.

Additionally, a density bonus allows developers to exceed height limits by up to 50% if at least 20% of the extra units are designated as affordable, below-market units.

The City of Raleigh approved an $80 million housing bond in 2020 that is projected to create at least 700 affordable homes, fund homebuyer assistance and help homeowners with home repairs.

About $14 million has already gone to four developments totaling more than 240 units, while another $24 million in gap financing will back over 470 additional units, more than 90% of which will be affordable to households earning 60% of area median income or less.

Between 2021 and 2024, Raleigh added 16,884 housing units, growing its housing stock by 7.7%, even as the city’s population grew by 5.8% over the same period. Raleigh’s housing growth also outpaced the state (5.7%) and national (3.2%) rates during that period.

In a recent development, of the 16,884 units added, roughly 2,000, or 12%, were affordable to households earning 80% or less of area median income (AMI), with Raleigh’s housing bond funds helping support their development. Density bonuses contributed about 200 of those affordable units, accounting for 10% of the total.

Industry observers note that additionally, Raleigh’s code changes intentionally shifted a large share of production away from detached single-family homes toward townhomes, duplexes and tiny homes. Since 2021, the city has issued more than twice as many townhouse permits as in 2015 to 2020, and has permitted more than 200 duplex units and over 200 accessory dwelling units (ADUs).

According to recent reports, as a result, average monthly rents rose at only half the national pace and fell in real, inflation-adjusted terms. Pew’s analysis estimates inflation-adjusted rents declined 15% from 2022 to 2025, and, as of 2025, the income needed to afford the city’s median rent dropped from 79% of AMI to 65%.

It has been revealed that raleigh’s experience mirrors a wider trend among fast-growing Sun Belt markets, where less restrictive zoning and fewer barriers to housing development have supported greater housing production and helped moderate housing costs. The South accounted for more than half of all U.S. housing starts between 2021 and 2025, while Sun Belt markets continue to lead the nation in rent and home price declines.

Industry observers note that according to Yardi Matrix’s October 2026 multifamily report, rents fell year over year in 12 major US markets. The Sun Belt accounted for ten of those, led by Austin, Houston, Nashville, Tampa and Phoenix. The for-sale market shows a similar pattern, with home prices dropping disproportionately in the Sun Belt while climbing in the Northeast and Midwest.

Industry News: Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • Sources indicate that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

Sources indicate that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The organization started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Sources indicate that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

It has been revealed that listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the manufacturer.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the organization to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has noted it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will revision the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

  • Claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the upcoming bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Sources indicate that anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software. With a new enhancement today, Claude now can tell developers when the code it has generated is ready to ship into production environments.

The company announced the launch of Claude Ship, which is a new suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals. The last one is the most interesting of those capabilities, because code reviews and fixes are nothing new for AI. But Claude’s ability to automatically approve code changes based on the policies predetermined by an organization’s developer team is a novel development that has not been seen before.

Claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the upcoming bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools. At those organizations, fresh code is being whipped up in double-quick time, and there are also AI agents for checking that code and providing fixes if it’s not working as hoped. But until now, the final review and approval process has always been performed by humans. Claude Ship changes that.

The idea is that human developers can delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they’re asking AI to create.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line,” Anthropic noted in a blog post. “But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code and we wanted everything after the pull request to move that fast too.”.

It has been revealed that anthropic mentioned Claude Ship consists of three parts. The first is Code Review, which is a tool that has been generally available for some time already. The other two are PR Steward and Claude Approvals, and they’re both still in beta. PR Steward is designed to handle issues such as failing continuous integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After each push, it will leave comments on what changes were made and how to roll them back if necessary.

Industry observers note that once PR Steward is done, Claude Approvals takes over. It works by applying an approval policy that’s left as a file in the codebase’s repository. The approval process can incorporate various elements, including the findings in Code Review and the organization’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Anthropic is urging early adopters to be cautious. Because Claude Ship is still in beta, it recommends running Claude Approvals in observe-only mode first. It also advises teams to begin with just one repository first, and set monthly spending limits so they can maintain more control over everything.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid rapidly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Industry observers note that underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he noted.

According to recent reports, he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

It has been revealed that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek remarked. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Sources indicate that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

In a recent development, after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk manufacturer developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

According to recent reports, “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

In a recent development, he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

In a recent development, redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

It has been revealed that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd remarked, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion organization Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

Sources indicate that A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The firm landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

According to recent reports, team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd mentioned he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

In a recent development, endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

Sources indicate that “This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

Georgia builders give affordable housing an essential fresh identity

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Put an affordable housing project on a planning commission agenda, and the neighborhood naysayers come out of the woodwork to fight.
  • They argue it will destroy the neighborhood’s character.
  • In a recent development, what’s in a name?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Put an affordable housing project on a planning commission agenda, and the neighborhood naysayers come out of the woodwork to fight.

They argue it will destroy the neighborhood’s character. Labeling the development as workforce housing doesn’t help much.

In a recent development, what’s in a name? An affordable home – or neighborhood – by any other name is still affordable, no? Still, companies rebrand when the current brand is struggling. And Georgia homebuilders and land developers are taking a crack at giving “affordable housing” a brand makeover, one that’s less stigma and more economic and social fabric dynamism.

The Georgia Residential Land Development Council and the Home Builders Association teamed up to dub affordable housing “essential homes.” They are pairing it with a tagline: “Homes for the people who keep Georgia working.”.

But defining essential homes as housing that workers can afford near where they work could be applied broadly as lawmakers from the federal to local levels wrestle with how to make housing more affordable.

“It’s a reality nationally that the buying power of the average American is not considered in land use and zoning policies,” Jay Knight, GRLDC’s chairman, told HousingWire TBD. “Essential homes for essential people intends to move the conversation from sticks and bricks allowed to the notable people being prohibited.”.

Sources indicate that the definition names no home size or price point. It asks whether the people who work in a community can afford to live there. Teachers, firefighters, nurses, first responders, healthcare workers and skilled tradespeople are among the livelihoods the term “essential” captures best. They also include younger Georgians hoping to buy a first home.

Austin Hackney, HBAG’s executive vice president, said in a statement that the term puts a human face on the affordability debate. He said that when workers can’t find homes within reach of their income, the effects reach employers, schools and local businesses.

The rebrand comes with a policy push. The groups say zoning restrictions, long permit reviews, infrastructure requirements and delayed final plat approvals add substantial costs that end up in home prices.

Sources indicate that GRLDC helped advance Senate Bill 447, which took effect July 1. The law sets timelines and accountability for Georgia’s land disturbance permit reviews. The council’s next target is final plat and bond reform. It wants reasonable approval timelines, standardized bonding requirements, and an end to delays that keep completed developments from moving forward.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development considers housing affordable when occupants pays no more than 30% of gross income on housing costs. Programs add other definitions, often tied to area median income. Affordable housing typically targets households at 60% of the area median income or less, while workforce housing covers roughly 60% to 120%.

Workforce housing, however, isn’t explicitly defined in federal law or regulation, according to a March 2026 Congressional Research Service analysis. But the term is used to avoid saying a housing development is affordable housing.

Opposition often centers on neighborhood character. Researchers also find residents may fear newcomers’ socioeconomic status more than the buildings themselves. Property values are another common worry, though research cited by the Florida Housing Coalition found almost no negative effect on neighboring market-rate homes.

Knight said the definition problem became clear at a speaking engagement. He asked a room of roughly 40 people to define affordable housing. One woman said Section 8. Someone else said anything under $400,000. A person from the Northeast thought it meant rent control.

According to recent reports, knight noted that convinced him people weren’t talking about the same thing, which made the conversation unproductive. His business partner suggested essential homes. Knight said the organizations liked it immediately.

According to recent reports, terms such as affordable homes, starter homes, first-time buyer or workforce housing arrive with a definition already attached. Knight noted “essential homes” encourages people to ask what it means, which gives the groups a chance to set the definition themselves.

The rationale behind the rebranding is that if local governments can dictate what can be built, the standard shouldn’t exceed what their own employees can buy. Knight said the average municipal employee earns about $60,000 to $62,000 a year in Georgia. That means they can afford about a $225,000 home.

In most U.S. markets today, that would buy roughly 1,100 square feet on a 35-foot detached lot, with no garage and no homeowners association, he said. He added that would put the price at about three and a half times annual income, close to the ratio GIs returning from World War II paid in the late 1940s and 1950s.

Knight stated zoning conditions have pushed home prices to a much higher ratio. High-cost areas like California, Upcoming York and Florida are prime examples. In Silicon Valley, the median home price is 11.4 times median household income, according to an annual report from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. The Miami metro’s ratio is 7.6.

High prices relative to income are a major reason the median first-time homebuyer is now 40. It’s an all-time high, according to the National Association of Realtors. Such a disparity is why California and Florida have been at the forefront of housing reforms.

According to recent reports, the Georgia campaign will put faces to the term: a police officer, a teacher, a nurse and a forklift operator. Knight said it will portray the kinds of workers that municipalities court with industry.

Knight, who sits on an advisory council for the National Association of Home Builders, stated he has shared the term with the executive director of the Houston Home Builders Association. He said Houston is now discussing it, since builders nationwide are having the same conversations.

“Who can be against essential housing?” Knight remarked.

The author pointed to Bitcoin's fixed supply. There will be only 21 million BTC in total, and about 20 million coins have already been mined, Kiyosaki wrote. "As far as I know, there has never been a 'money' such as Bitcoin ever before," he added.

"With price of Bitcoin crashing, I can't wait to buy more coins… just because only 21 million are ever to be mined. It could be a 'nothing burger'…. or the best money I've ever spent," Kiyosaki wrote.

In late August, Kiyosaki said on podcasts that he owed creditors $1.2 billion. His ex-wife and business partner, Kim Kiyosaki, later said that the figure covered the loans of a partnership that owns about 1,500 rental units. "We have a lot of apartment houses with our partners," she said.

According to Kim Kiyosaki, Robert Kiyosaki's own share of the debt is $30 million to $60 million. Each of their real estate investments is held in a separate LLC. Robert Kiyosaki also commented on the debt at the time. "If it all comes to hell, you can talk to my attorney," he mentioned.

In 2012, Kiyosaki's company Rich Global LLC filed for bankruptcy after a court ordered it to pay about $24 million.

Breaking: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Industry observers note that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Industry observers note that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Massive Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft claims the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

It has been revealed that the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in upcoming hires.

Recent findings suggest that the worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the firm decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

Recent findings suggest that there is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

In a recent development, one of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

In a recent development, but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one manufacturer.

According to recent reports, hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

Recent findings suggest that AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual manufacturer. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software manufacturer.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a firm.

Industry observers note that software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

Recent findings suggest that this cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue rapidly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

Sources indicate that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY massive, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

According to recent reports, 2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a organization that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

Industry observers note that 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

Industry observers note that there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a organization of their own or a year with their family.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BlackRock, the leading asset management firm and Bitcoin’s largest ETF issuer, sparked discussions earlier today following a massive Bitcoin sale by the company.

The latest data showcased by SosoValue shows that the leading Bitcoin fund has witnessed massive single-day withdrawals from investors who have ventured into its Bitcoin investment product.

Earlier today, BlackRock sold over half a billion dollars’ worth of Bitcoin after its spot Bitcoin ETF, also known as iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), recorded a total of $541.08 million in net outflows.

This massive outflow has come as Bitcoin’s price decline continues to intensify, causing investors to aggressively pull their money out of the fund amid growing market fear.

While this marks the third time this week that BlackRock has recorded a net outflow amid persistent market volatility, it also marks the largest single-day outflow BlackRock has recorded since its launch.

Apparently, the record-breaking withdrawal that the fund just witnessed suggests that institutional and traditional investors are becoming less willing to retain their exposure to Bitcoin through asset managers, especially as Bitcoin’s price continues to slump further.

Although BlackRock has just suffered the largest withdrawal since it launched its Bitcoin investment product, the record outflow did not alter its dominance in the market.

Further data indicates that the BlackRock spot Bitcoin ETF still boasts a massive $47.82 billion in assets under management, spotlighting its leadership in the Bitcoin ETF market.

This positions it far ahead of Fidelity, which ranks as the second-largest Bitcoin ETF with just $10.62 billion in net assets.
